summary: Joel 1 opens with Yahweh’s word to Joel and a call for elders and inhabitants of the land to recognize a disaster unlike anything in living memory. Successive devouring swarms have ruined the harvest, interrupting offerings and stripping away joy. The chapter moves from public shock to mourning, fasting, and Joel’s cry to Yahweh as fields, animals, water brooks, and pastures fail.
whyItMatters: This chapter establishes the book’s starting point: a ruined harvest is not treated as a private misfortune but as a crisis touching worship, work, memory, land, and animals. It introduces the “day of Yahweh” as near before the later chapters turn toward return, restoration, and judgment.

context.author: The heading identifies Joel, the son of Pethuel, as the one to whom Yahweh’s word came; it gives no further biography.
context.audience: The chapter addresses elders, all inhabitants of the land, drinkers of wine, farmers, vineyard keepers, priests, and ministers of the altar in Judah’s worshiping community.
context.date: The book is undated. A postexilic date is a substantial scholarly proposal, but the heading names no king or reign.
context.setting: The book places the crisis in Judah and Jerusalem. Here, crop loss links fields and vineyards with the interrupted worship at Yahweh’s house.
context.literaryForm: Prophetic lament and summons, using urgent commands, poetic description, and public mourning language.

outline.heading: The word and the remembered disaster
outline.note: Joel is named, the elders and inhabitants are told to hear, and the devastation is described as something to tell future generations.

outline.heading: Wine, vine, and fig tree stripped
outline.note: Drinkers are called to wake and weep because the sweet wine is cut off, while the invader is pictured with lion-like teeth and the vines and fig trees are ruined.

outline.heading: Mourning reaches Yahweh’s house
outline.note: The chapter calls for mourning like bereavement because offerings have stopped, priests mourn, and grain, wine, and oil fail.

outline.heading: Farmers, trees, and joy wither
outline.note: Farmers and vineyard keepers are told to wail as wheat, barley, vines, fruit trees, and human joy wither together.

outline.heading: Priests are told to gather the people
outline.note: Priests and ministers are commanded to mourn in sackcloth, sanctify a fast, call a solemn assembly, gather the people, and cry to Yahweh.

outline.heading: The day of Yahweh and the collapsing land
outline.note: The approaching day is named as destruction, and the chapter ends with food, joy, seeds, barns, livestock, water brooks, trees, and pastures all caught in the crisis as Joel cries to Yahweh.

keyVerses.text: Tell your children about it, and have your children tell their children, and their children, another generation.
keyVerses.why: The disaster is framed as a memory the community must pass on, not merely a bad season to forget.

keyVerses.text: What the swarming locust has left, the great locust has eaten. What the great locust has left, the grasshopper has eaten. What the grasshopper has left, the caterpillar has eaten.
keyVerses.why: This verse gives the chapter’s central image of repeated, cumulative loss.

keyVerses.text: Sanctify a fast. Call a solemn assembly. Gather the elders and all the inhabitants of the land to the house of Yahweh, your God, and cry to Yahweh.
keyVerses.why: The response to the crisis is to involve the whole community: elders and inhabitants are called to gather at Yahweh’s house and cry out.

keyVerses.text: Alas for the day! For the day of Yahweh is at hand, and it will come as destruction from the Almighty.
keyVerses.why: The chapter connects the present devastation with the larger theme of the day of Yahweh, which continues through the book.

questions.question: Who is Joel, and what do we know about him here?
questions.answer: The heading identifies Joel as the son of Pethuel and the recipient of Yahweh’s word. It gives no hometown, office, king, or date, leaving his personal biography largely unknown.

questions.question: Why are the elders and all the inhabitants told to listen?
questions.answer: The opening summons treats the disaster as a public event that the whole land must consider. The question, “Has this ever happened in your days, or in the days of your fathers?” presents it as an unusually severe crisis. Verse 3 then turns the event into something to be told to future generations.

questions.question: Are the locusts literal insects or a picture of an invading army?
questions.answer: Joel 1 describes crop devastation through four consuming terms and then says “a nation has come up on my land.” Readers differ on how far the military image should be pressed. In this chapter, the clear point is overwhelming destruction of vines, fig trees, grain, wine, oil, and trees, whether the language is read as insects described like invaders or as an invasion pictured through locust-like devastation.

questions.question: What is “sackcloth”?
questions.answer: Sackcloth is clothing associated with mourning. Verse 8 compares the community’s grief to that of a young woman mourning the husband of her youth; verse 13 directly tells priests to wear sackcloth and lie in it all night. The comparison and the command make grief public and visible.

questions.question: Why does the loss of crops affect Yahweh’s house?
questions.answer: The chapter says the meal offering and drink offering are cut off from Yahweh’s house. Grain, wine, and oil are not only food and livelihood here; they are also connected with worship. The agricultural collapse therefore reaches the priests and the altar as well as the fields.

questions.question: Does Joel 1 say what sin caused the disaster?
questions.answer: Joel calls the people to mourn, fast, assemble, and cry to Yahweh, but he does not identify a specific offense by Judah. The day of Yahweh gives the crisis a threatening religious meaning without supplying a list of sins. The passage therefore provides no basis for assigning a particular blame to people suffering a present-day disaster.

questions.question: Why does verse 17 mention seeds in one translation and animals in another?
questions.answer: WEB describes seeds rotting under clods, while Douay-Rheims describes beasts rotting in dung and Brenton describes heifers starting at their mangers. The Hebrew wording is unusually difficult, so the exact objects and actions remain disputed. The surrounding ruined storehouses and withered grain place the line within the same agricultural collapse.

questions.question: What does “the day of Yahweh” mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: Verse 15 says the day of Yahweh is near and will come as destruction from the Almighty. In Joel 1, that phrase is tied to the present scene of food cut off, joy removed from God’s house, grain ruined, animals groaning, and water dried up. Later parts of Joel develop the phrase further, but this chapter introduces it through disaster and alarm.

questions.question: Why do animals and the land matter so much in the final verses?
questions.answer: The chapter does not limit the crisis to human hunger or religious loss. Herds groan, livestock are perplexed, sheep are desolate, animals pant, water brooks dry up, and pastures are devoured. The closing picture shows a whole living environment caught in the disaster as Joel cries to Yahweh.

glossary.def: A mourning garment in this chapter; both the bereaved image in verse 8 and the priests in verse 13 are associated with it.
An offering from the produce of the land; Joel says it is cut off or withheld from Yahweh’s house because the agricultural supply has failed.
An offering connected here with wine; its absence shows that the ruined harvest has interrupted worship.
A public gathering called in verse 14, where elders and inhabitants of the land are gathered to Yahweh’s house to cry to Yahweh.
The near day named in verse 15, described in this chapter as coming with destruction from the Almighty.
